title: Compute-in-memory implementation of state space models for event sequence processing

paper_content.abstract: State space models have recently emerged as a powerful framework for long sequence processing, outperforming traditional methods on diverse benchmarks. Fundamentally, state space models can generalize both recurrent and convolutional networks and have been shown to even capture key functions of biological systems. Here we report an approach to implement SSMs in energy-efficient compute-in-memory hardware to achieve real-time, event-driven processing. Our work re-parameterizes the model to function with real-valued coefficients and shared decay constants, reducing the complexity of model mapping onto practical hardware systems. By leveraging device dynamics and diagonalized state transition parameters, the state evolution can be natively implemented in crossbar-based compute-in-memory systems combined with memristors exhibiting short-term memory effects. Through this algorithm and hardware co-design, we show the proposed system offers both high accuracy and high energy efficiency while supporting fully asynchronous processing for event-based vision and audio tasks.

We performed several additional analyses in simulation to analyze the model behavior. Figure 3a–d show how the classification accuracy evolves as we vary the number of stacked SSM blocks (model depth) for different event-driven datasets. All models tested employ the same underlying architecture differing mainly in the number of stacked SSM blocks after the embedding layer. We observe that increasing the depth initially enhances performance, reflecting the model’s ability to better capture complex temporal dynamics with more layers. However, this improvement reaches a saturation point, typically around 6 blocks, indicating that adding further SSM blocks beyond a certain threshold yields minimal or no accuracy gain. The saturation effect is common in neural networks-beyond an optimal depth, adding more layers may offer diminishing returns and can increase the risk of overfitting or optimization difficulties during training. Therefore, the design of our model architecture is based on the saturation point. We note the required depth (about 6 blocks) is remarkably shallow compared to many conventional deep networks. For example, Bulzomi et al.46 and Gehrig et al.47 use ResNet48 as the model backbone for the DVS datasets which employs more than 30 layers. The fact that SSMs can effectively model long-range event sequences with just 6 blocks underscore their representational efficiency and make them particularly attractive for hardware deployment, where model mapping complexity and latency scale roughly with layer count.

To evaluate the effects of constraining the decay parameter to a single value per block, we compare the final classification accuracies across four event-driven datasets-two audio datasets and two vision- based datasets under conditions where the decay parameter \lambda is either freely learned (unfixed) or held constant (fixed), shown in Fig. 3e. For most datasets, we observe that fixing \lambda following the approach discussed in the Model Training section surprisingly results in improved accuracy by approximately 1% on average. Specifically, SHD improves from 94.7% to 95.7%, DVS128 Gesture from 96.6% to 97.3%, and DVS128 Lips from 61.1% to 63.5%. Notably, the Spiking Speech Commands (SSC) dataset exhibits a critical failure when \lambda is unfixed, leading to divergent training with invalid Nota Number (NAN) loss values, yet it achieves a stable and competitive accuracy of 84.7% when \lambda is fixed. These observations indicate that constraining \lambda may in fact help stabilize training convergence by serving as a form of regularization for event-driven datasets, including those with challenging temporal structures such as SSC.

To further investigate the instability observed in SSC, we plot in Fig. 3f the distribution of \tau = 1/\lambda across the SSM layers for SSC and other datasets. Since training with unconstrained \lambda on the SSC dataset terminated prematurely due to NAN values, the \tau values plotted here for SSC were recorded from the final stable iteration immediately before divergence occurred. Notably, on SSC \tau values are significantly larger compared to the other datasets, indicating slower decay rates in the hidden states. From a continuous-time perspective, the hidden state updates following:

h(t+ \Delta t) = exp(- \Delta t / \tau) h(t), (9)

With larger \tau, the hidden state h decays more slowly, preserving more historical information over prolonged periods. While beneficial for capturing long-term dependencies, this slow decay can cause the hidden states to accumulate excessively when the input event rate is high, which is also the case for SSC. Consequently, gradients and loss values can become unstable, resulting in divergence and NAN values. This numerical instability illustrates the challenges associated with unconstrained optimization of \lambda on datasets with demanding temporal characteristics, and the necessity of carefully regularizing \lambda to maintain numerical stability and achieve convergence.

HardwareSystemPerformanceAnalysis
We next evaluate the model implementation on CIM hardware using the SSC and DVS-Gesture datasets. To align the SSM model with analog CIM hardware constraints, all weights and activations are quantized to 8-bit integer (INT8) using quantization-aware training49,50. This step causes no accuracy degradation for the DVS-Gesture model (remaining at 97.3%) and only a minimal 0.3% drop for the SSC model (from 84.7% to 84.4%).

We then studied the effect of device non-idealities in analog hardware by introducing random hardware variations to the INT8 parameters (see Method) based on the measured device variation effect data in Fig. 2b–d. This resulted in only a modest accuracy decline for both models without any re-training or other mitigation techniques: the SSC accuracy dropped 2.39% to 82.01%, and the DVS-Gesture accuracy dropped 2.2% to 95.1%. Since the STM memristors need to implement the trained \lambda, we also analyzed the effects of variations in the device decay rate on model performance (Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Note 3). These results show that the models exhibit negligible accuracy degradation with variations up to 10% of the mean, without any re-training or variation-aware training techniques. The noise and variation analyses support the resilience of the proposed model for practical analog hardware implementations, likely due to the use of only fully-connect layers and the shallow model architecture. Future implementation of techniques such as variation-aware-training50 is expected to further improve the hardware accuracy.

To estimate power consumption, we constructed simulation for the proposed hardware system for the SSC dataset, using experimentally measured data from the CIM chip and STM memristor devices for the SSC dataset. The system consists of 6 SSM blocks, as shown in Fig. 4a.

The total power consumption for our system is estimated to be 34mW and the energy distribution across system components is shown in Fig. 4b (see Method). The 8-bit ADCs dominate the power budget, accounting for 43.7% of total power usage. Analog power consumption in the RRAM arrays follow, consuming 30.3%. SN devices for update behaviors consume 0.4%. However, we note that the estimate was based on ADCs and other digital components constantly operating at 40MHz due to the limitations of the current CIM chip. In practice, when the operations are truly operated in an event-driven fashion, the ADCs will not be active all the time and actual power consumption can be significantly lower. The power can be further improved by eliminating the analog-digital transitions to implement all operations in the analog domain, which is compatible with SSM based approaches.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript entitled ‘Compute-in-Memory Implementation of State Space Models for Event Sequence Processing’ presents a SSM & CIM co-design method to implement efficient asynchronous processing for event sequences. This work is noteworthy in replacing the numeric iteration in the SSM with the short term memory effect of WOx devices, while using RRAM for VMM operations. The authors claimed that the proposed method outperforms existing SNN-based methods with respect to benchmark performance and power. However, the manuscript exhibits several weaknesses that require further improvement, as detailed below.
1) The authors present their method as a real-time, event-driven hardware system. Therefore, it is expected to demonstrate a complete system with sufficient design details and measurement results. Critical parts should include the WOx-based SSM block, RRAM-based embedding layer and VMM modules, as well as how they work (e.g., how to implement line 338-341 physically?). Fig. 1 and 3 show several highly abstracted figures without details, making a big gap between the proposed concept and the hardware implementation. Moreover, the CIM chip of Fig. 3(A) is the only hardware image I can find in this paper, and again, without any details. It is suggested to provide a more thorough documentation of the hardware implementation to allow readers to follow.
2) It is not clear whether the results in Table 1 and 2 were obtained through simulation or hardware measurement. Please clarify in both caption and main text. It is hard to “imagine” the deployment of millions of parameters onto the proposed system without knowing the implementation details. If it was done by simulation, please provide full details about the simulation model, e.g. how was the noise modelled?
3) Following the last comment, please clearly present the data source throughout the manuscript. It is known the figure 3(C), (D) and S2 were experimentally measured, while fig 4(B) was simulated by TSMC PDK. What about other data, e.g. Fig 2? For the above reasons, it is hard to tell weather the results are technically sound.
4) The authors are mixing multiple concepts, which may hinder reader comprehension. The term Reservoir Node should originate from reservoir computing. The authors previously published reservoir computing works with the same device WOx and the same decay property (ref. 58). As the decay factor (cid:1) in eq. 2 and 9 are determined by the WOx devices, it is fixed and less likely to be trained. Therefore the definition appears to be in line with reservoir computing. In fact, reservoir computing can be considered a SSM as the reservoir layer produces a state space. The authors should clarify the necessity of this new terminology and discuss how their SSM-based approach different from reservoir computing frameworks.
5) The training process could be described in more detail. Please provide more details about the implementation of BPTT and how it handles the noisy dynamical behavior of WOx and RRAM? Are they differentiable? Also, it would be helpful to show the loss curve for the tasks.
6) The authors claimed fully asynchronous processing. But, could the authors clarify how the claimed asynchronicity is maintained given that the ADC/DAC likely require clocks? The extent of asynchronicity needs to be clarified.
7) In Line 374, the authors didn’t explain how to measure the power of RN devices and CIM chip. This is an important part that would benefit from more details.
8) Both figures and text are poorly organized. The main problems are:
(i) fig 1 (B) and (C) are somewhat unclear. Why the embedding vector is pointed to a straight line? It is not understood what exactly is the embedding. Both captions mention ‘internal structure’. The current figures may illustrate some functionalities but the structure is not clearly depicted.
(ii) Insufficient labeling in figures obscures essential experimental/design details. The authors should label all the terms. For instance, what are delta t1 and delta t2 in Fig 1(c)? What does every arrow means in fig 4(A)? In fig. 4(B), the power distribution percentages quoted in the text (lines 387-389) do not match those shown in Figure 4(B). And What is LUT? It has not been mentioned throughout the text. In table 2, the acc. for DVS128 is 63.5%, that is, different from the 62.8% in line 280. Please double check the paper.
(iii) It is suggested to totally reorganize the Results and Methods section. The majority of line 121-145 looks like a figure caption. And there are too many method descriptions in the Result section. Please first clear up what information should be in the Results, Methods, figure caption and SI, and then rewrite accordingly.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper presents a methodology for implementing SSMs on CIM hardware, and holds significant potential by crossing over two emerging fields. In my view, this paper can enable significant impact. Some minor notes that could enhance the quality and technical accuracy of the manuscript are provided below. Note there are several references used to back up several points in this review. I do not expect the authors to include these citations.
Introduction
- The authors state that the use of surrogate gradients is what compromises model accuracy. While this is broadly the accepted view and commonly cited reason, I'd contend that surrogate gradients are generally quite robust (especially in the era of QAT and extreme low-precision models that have been shown to scale up). I expect the main limiter is binarization of activations. This drives excessive information compression. This constraint is highlighted in Zhu et al.'s work in SpikeGPT (TMLR, 2024).
- The paragraph that highlights the mismatch for convolutions and transformers for CIM makes a lot of sense. Buchel & Sebastian et al.'s work in "Efficient scaling of large language models with mixture of experts and 3D analog in-memory computing", Nat Comp Sci, 2025 is a good reference for this, where all Transformer/self-attention operations are delegated to digital circuitry. However, an additional challenge is that applying CIM to dense-layers alone does not address the primary bottleneck of Transformer ops for long sequence length. I.e., Transformers will dominate the computational cost relative to dense layers. This paragraph (or the start of the following paragraph) could be made more compelling by more clearly stating that SSMs overcome the memory-bottleneck of self-attention/KV-caching, making them a natural fit for CIM architectures.
- There is some tightly related work where SSMs are deployed on neuromorphic/event-based hardware by Abreu et al. (Neuromorphic Principles for Efficient Large Language Models on Intel Loihi 2, ICLR SCOPE Workshop, 2025) & Zhu et al. (Scalable MatMul-Free Language Modeling on Neuromorphic Hardware, arXiv 2025). Neither uses CIM, and instead relies on digital, async accelerators.
- I would encourage citing the original SSM+DL work by Voelker, Kajic & Eliasmith, "Legendre memory units: Continuous-time representation in recurrent neural networks", neurips, 2018, where referring to "grounded in control theory".
- The use of real-valued coefficients in the transition matrix is acceptable, and the use of non-dynamic/input-dependent transition matrices for the update is a fair fit for CIM, though the dynamic transition matrix is a big part of what boosts performance in recurrent architectures. I think it is fair to state frankly that this is a limitation, although, if it was delegated to digital computation, it's a tiny fraction of the overall compute.
Results
- The graph in Figure 1(B) is a unclear to me (the square).
- The discussion on nonlinearities could use the phrase "positional nonlinearity" which 1) preserves universal function approximation, 2) without breaking the ability to represent training as 1D-conv.
- In model training, it's said that BPTT is used. Training an SSM is indeed functionally equivalent to BPTT, though some folk take issue with it as BPTT is defined as having linear time complexity while training SSMs follows log-complexity with time. I don't think there is concrete guidance here - I have no fixation on this if you prefer not to change this.
- It is unclear to me where the asynchronousity in the SSM comes from. What is sparsifying the activations?
- While not essential, an ablation study to identify what features of the RRAM/ADC non-idealities impact performance.
- There is limited information on how sparsity provides an advantage in this particular set up.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript presents an algorithm-hardware co-design approach for efficient, real-time, and asynchronous processing using state space models (SSMs). The key contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) a re-parameterized 6-block SSM model in which the decay parameter (λ) is shared within each block, thereby reducing hardware complexity while improving accuracy; (2) a memristor-based compute-in-memory (CIM) architecture to accelerate input vector-matrix multiplications (VMMs); and (3) an exploitation of the intrinsic short-term conductance decay behavior of memristors to perform hidden state (h) updates. However, several parts of the manuscript lack clarity and require further elaboration and justification.
1. Recent References on RRAM CIM
The reference list regarding RRAM CIM could be strengthened by including recent works published in Nature and Nature Electronics. Incorporating these high-impact studies would better position the manuscript within the current state of the art and highlight its relevance to ongoing developments.
2. Crossbar vs. 1T1R Structures
The manuscript should address the impact of sneak current in crossbar arrays and provide a discussion comparing the advantages and trade-offs of crossbar versus 1T1R structures. Such an analysis would help readers better appreciate the design choices and their implications for scalability and reliability.
3. Figure 1(A) & (B): Clarity of Asynchronous Event Representation
The presentation of asynchronous events through the channel-wise embedding layer is unclear. For instance, the y-axis values are not specified, and it is difficult to determine whether the spikes in (A) correspond directly to the square wave in (B). Providing clarification or additional explanation would greatly improve readability.
4. Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Processing
The manuscript emphasizes the importance of asynchronous processing, but the distinction from synchronous processing is not sufficiently detailed. The authors are encouraged to elaborate on the differences, including their respective advantages and disadvantages. For example, in Table 2, Peng et al. [50] report comparable performance despite not being asynchronous. Enhancing this comparison table to highlight the significance of the proposed approach would strengthen the manuscript.
5. Figure 2(A–D): Caption and Interpretation
The caption states “Analysis of model architecture and decay parameter (λ) choices on classification accuracy,” yet the figure appears to show the number of blocks versus accuracy. Does the caption misstate the content, or is there a specific relationship between λ and the number of blocks? Furthermore, the authors claim that the proposed model requires only six blocks, whereas counterparts such as ResNet require more than 30 layers. Given the distinction between the terms “block” and “layer,” is it valid to conclude that the proposed model achieves lower latency? A direct comparison in terms of latency or other performance metrics would make this claim more convincing.
6. RRAM Mapping Strategy
The authors map positive and negative weights onto separate RRAM arrays, while prior work often employs 2’s complement mapping, requiring only a single array. What motivated the use of separate arrays in this work? Discussion of the resulting area overhead and associated trade-offs would add valuable context.
7. Fixed Decay Parameter (λ) and Accuracy
Line 276 states that inference accuracy improves when fixing the decay parameter (λ). The authors should provide a more detailed mathematical derivation or theoretical explanation to clarify why and how fixing λ enhances accuracy.
8. Flexibility Limitations of Memristor Conductance Decay
Using memristor conductance decay as RN is an intriguing approach. However, because the decay rate is largely determined by oxide thickness during fabrication, flexibility may be limited for supporting different SSM models or enabling weight updates. The authors should elaborate on potential solutions to overcome this limitation, particularly given the importance of reprogramming capabilities at the edge.
9. Voltage Levels and Endurance in Conductance Updates
In Equation (9), the horizontal line voltages of the input projection memristor array are used as input spikes x(t+Δt) to update conductance. The authors should clarify the voltage levels applied in this process. Moreover, since each conductance update effectively involves multiple write operations, a discussion of endurance concerns under repeated updates would be valuable.

## Abstract

State space models have recently emerged as a powerful framework for long sequence processing, outperforming traditional methods on diverse benchmarks. Fundamentally, state space models can generalize both recurrent and convolutional networks and have been shown to even capture key functions of biological systems. Here we report an approach to implement SSMs in energy-efficient compute-in-memory hardware to achieve real-time, event-driven processing. Our work re-parameterizes the model to function with real-valued coefficients and shared decay constants, reducing the complexity of model mapping onto practical hardware systems. By leveraging device dynamics and diagonalized state transition parameters, the state evolution can be natively implemented in crossbar-based compute-in-memory systems combined with memristors exhibiting short-term memory effects. Through this algorithm and hardware co-design, we show the proposed system offers both high accuracy and high energy efficiency while supporting fully asynchronous processing for event-based vision and audio tasks.

We performed several additional analyses in simulation to analyze the model behavior. Figure 3a–d show how the classification accuracy evolves as we vary the number of stacked SSM blocks (model depth) for different event-driven datasets. All models tested employ the same underlying architecture differing mainly in the number of stacked SSM blocks after the embedding layer. We observe that increasing the depth initially enhances performance, reflecting the model’s ability to better capture complex temporal dynamics with more layers. However, this improvement reaches a saturation point, typically around 6 blocks, indicating that adding further SSM blocks beyond a certain threshold yields minimal or no accuracy gain. The saturation effect is common in neural networks-beyond an optimal depth, adding more layers may offer diminishing returns and can increase the risk of overfitting or optimization difficulties during training. Therefore, the design of our model architecture is based on the saturation point. We note the required depth (about 6 blocks) is remarkably shallow compared to many conventional deep networks. For example, Bulzomi et al.46 and Gehrig et al.47 use ResNet48 as the model backbone for the DVS datasets which employs more than 30 layers. The fact that SSMs can effectively model long-range event sequences with just 6 blocks underscore their representational efficiency and make them particularly attractive for hardware deployment, where model mapping complexity and latency scale roughly with layer count.

For most datasets, we observe that fixing \lambda following the approach discussed in the Model Training section surprisingly results in improved accuracy by approximately 1% on average. Specifically, SHD improves from 94.7% to 95.7%, DVS128 Gesture from 96.6% to 97.3%, and DVS128 Lips from 61.1% to 63.5%. Notably, the Spiking Speech Commands (SSC) dataset exhibits a critical failure when \lambda is unfixed, leading to divergent training with invalid Nota Number (NAN) loss values, yet it achieves a stable and competitive accuracy of 84.7% when \lambda is fixed. These observations indicate that constraining \lambda may in fact help stabilize training convergence by serving as a form of regularization for event-driven datasets, including those with challenging temporal structures such as SSC.

To further investigate the instability observed in SSC, we plot in Fig. 3f the distribution of \tau = 1/\lambda across the SSM layers for SSC and other datasets. Since training with unconstrained \lambda on the SSC dataset terminated prematurely due to NAN values, the \tau values plotted here for SSC were recorded from the final stable iteration immediately before divergence occurred. Notably, on SSC \tau values are significantly larger compared to the other datasets, indicating slower decay rates in the hidden states. From a continuous-time perspective, the hidden state updates following:

h(t+ \Delta t) = exp(- \Delta t / \tau) h(t), (9)

With larger \tau, the hidden state h decays more slowly, preserving more historical information over prolonged periods. While beneficial for capturing long-term dependencies, this slow decay can cause the hidden states to accumulate excessively when the input event rate is high, which is also the case for SSC. Consequently, gradients and loss values can become unstable, resulting in divergence and NAN values. This numerical instability illustrates the challenges associated with unconstrained optimization of \lambda on datasets with demanding temporal characteristics, and the necessity of carefully regularizing \lambda to maintain numerical stability and achieve convergence.

We next evaluate the model implementation on CIM hardware using the SSC and DVS-Gesture datasets. To align the SSM model with analog CIM hardware constraints, all weights and activations are quantized to 8-bit integer (INT8) using quantization-aware training49,50. This step causes no accuracy degradation for the DVS-Gesture model (remaining at 97.3%) and only a minimal 0.3% drop for the SSC model (from 84.7% to 84.4%).

We then studied the effect of device non-idealities in analog hardware by introducing random hardware variations to the INT8 parameters (see Method) based on the measured device variation effect data in Fig. 2b–d. This resulted in only a modest accuracy decline for both models without any re-training or other mitigation techniques: the SSC accuracy dropped 2.39% to 82.01%, and the DVS-Gesture accuracy dropped 2.2% to 95.1%. Since the STM memristors need to implement the trained \lambda, we also analyzed the effects of variations in the device decay rate on model performance (Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Note 3). These results show that the models exhibit negligible accuracy degradation with variations up to 10% of the mean, without any re-training or variation-aware training techniques. The noise and variation analyses support the resilience of the proposed model for practical analog hardware implementations, likely due to the use of only fully-connect layers and the shallow model architecture. Future implementation of techniques such as variation-aware-training50 is expected to further improve the hardware accuracy.

To estimate power consumption, we constructed simulation for the proposed hardware system for the SSC dataset, using experimentally measured data from the CIM chip and STM memristor devices for the SSC dataset. The system consists of 6 SSM blocks, as shown in Fig. 4a.

The total power consumption for our system is estimated to be 34mW and the energy distribution across system components is shown in Fig. 4b (see Method). The 8-bit ADCs dominate the power budget, accounting for 43.7% of total power usage. Analog power consumption in the RRAM arrays follow, consuming 30.3%. SN devices for update behaviors consume 0.4%. However, we note that the estimate was based on ADCs and other digital components constantly operating at 40MHz due to the limitations of the current CIM chip. In practice, when the operations are truly operated in an event-driven fashion, the ADCs will not be active all the time and actual power consumption can be significantly lower. The power can be further improved by eliminating the analog-digital transitions to implement all operations in the analog domain, which is compatible with SSM based approaches.

The manuscript entitled ‘Compute-in-Memory Implementation of State Space Models for Event Sequence Processing’ presents a SSM & CIM co-design method to implement efficient asynchronous processing for event sequences. This work is noteworthy in replacing the numeric iteration in the SSM with the short term memory effect of WOx devices, while using RRAM for VMM operations. The authors claimed that the proposed method outperforms existing SNN-based methods with respect to benchmark performance and power. However, the manuscript exhibits several weaknesses that require further improvement, as detailed below.
1) The authors present their method as a real-time, event-driven hardware system. Therefore, it is expected to demonstrate a complete system with sufficient design details and measurement results. Critical parts should include the WOx-based SSM block, RRAM-based embedding layer and VMM modules, as well as how they work (e.g., how to implement line 338-341 physically?). Fig. 1 and 3 show several highly abstracted figures without details, making a big gap between the proposed concept and the hardware implementation. Moreover, the CIM chip of Fig. 3(A) is the only hardware image I can find in this paper, and again, without any details. It is suggested to provide a more thorough documentation of the hardware implementation to allow readers to follow.
2) It is not clear whether the results in Table 1 and 2 were obtained through simulation or hardware measurement. Please clarify in both caption and main text. It is hard to “imagine” the deployment of millions of parameters onto the proposed system without knowing the implementation details. If it was done by simulation, please provide full details about the simulation model, e.g. how was the noise modelled?

It is known the figure 3(C), (D) and S2 were experimentally measured, while fig 4(B) was simulated by TSMC PDK. What about other data, e.g. Fig 2? ### Reviewer 2

This paper presents a methodology for implementing SSMs on CIM hardware, and holds significant potential by crossing over two emerging fields. In my view, this paper can enable significant impact. Some minor notes that could enhance the quality and technical accuracy of the manuscript are provided below. Note there are several references used to back up several points in this review. I do not expect the authors to include these citations.
Introduction
- The authors state that the use of surrogate gradients is what compromises model accuracy. While this is broadly the accepted view and commonly cited reason, I'd contend that surrogate gradients are generally quite robust (especially in the era of QAT and extreme low-precision models that have been shown to scale up). I expect the main limiter is binarization of activations. This drives excessive information compression. This constraint is highlighted in Zhu et al.'s work in SpikeGPT (TMLR, 2024).
- The paragraph that highlights the mismatch for convolutions and transformers for CIM makes a lot of sense. Buchel & Sebastian et al.'s work in "Efficient scaling of large language models with mixture of experts and 3D analog in-memory computing", Nat Comp Sci, 2025 is a good reference for this, where all Transformer/self-attention operations are delegated to digital circuitry. However, an additional challenge is that applying CIM to dense-layers alone does not address the primary bottleneck of Transformer ops for long sequence length. I.e., Transformers will dominate the computational cost relative to dense layers. This paragraph (or the start of the following paragraph) could be made more compelling by more clearly stating that SSMs overcome the memory-bottleneck of self-attention/KV-caching, making them a natural fit for CIM architectures.
- There is some tightly related work where SSMs are deployed on neuromorphic/event-based hardware by Abreu et al. (Neuromorphic Principles for Efficient Large Language Models on Intel Loihi 2, ICLR SCOPE Workshop, 2025) & Zhu et al. (Scalable MatMul-Free Language Modeling on Neuromorphic Hardware, arXiv 2025). Neither uses CIM, and instead relies on digital, async accelerators.
- I would encourage citing the original SSM+DL work by Voelker, Kajic & Eliasmith, "Legendre memory units: Continuous-time representation in recurrent neural networks", neurips, 2018, where referring to "grounded in control theory".
- The use of real-valued coefficients in the transition matrix is acceptable, and the use of non-dynamic/input-dependent transition matrices for the update is a fair fit for CIM, though the dynamic transition matrix is a big part of what boosts performance in recurrent architectures. I think it is fair to state frankly that this is a limitation, although, if it was delegated to digital computation, it's a tiny fraction of the overall compute.
Results
- The graph in Figure 1(B) is a unclear to me (the square).
- The discussion on nonlinearities could use the phrase "positional nonlinearity" which 1) preserves universal function approximation, 2) without breaking the ability to represent training as 1D-conv.
- In model training, it's said that BPTT is used. Training an SSM is indeed functionally equivalent to BPTT, though some folk take issue with it as BPTT is defined as having linear time complexity while training SSMs follows log-complexity with time. I don't think there is concrete guidance here - I have no fixation on this if you prefer not to change this.
- It is unclear to me where the asynchronousity in the SSM comes from. What is sparsifying the activations?
- While not essential, an ablation study to identify what features of the RRAM/ADC non-idealities impact performance.
- There is limited information on how sparsity provides an advantage in this particular set up.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents an algorithm-hardware co-design approach for efficient, real-time, and asynchronous processing using state space models (SSMs). The key contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) a re-parameterized 6-block SSM model in which the decay parameter (λ) is shared within each block, thereby reducing hardware complexity while improving accuracy; (2) a memristor-based compute-in-memory (CIM) architecture to accelerate input vector-matrix multiplications (VMMs); and (3) an exploitation of the intrinsic short-term conductance decay behavior of memristors to perform hidden state (h) updates. However, several parts of the manuscript lack clarity and require further elaboration and justification.
1. Recent References on RRAM CIM
The reference list regarding RRAM CIM could be strengthened by including recent works published in Nature and Nature Electronics. Incorporating these high-impact studies would better position the manuscript within the current state of the art and highlight its relevance to ongoing developments.
2. Crossbar vs. 1T1R Structures
The manuscript should address the impact of sneak current in crossbar arrays and provide a discussion comparing the advantages and trade-offs of crossbar versus 1T1R structures. Such an analysis would help readers better appreciate the design choices and their implications for scalability and reliability.
3. Figure 1(A) & (B): Clarity of Asynchronous Event Representation
The presentation of asynchronous events through the channel-wise embedding layer is unclear. For instance, the y-axis values are not specified, and it is difficult to determine whether the spikes in (A) correspond directly to the square wave in (B). Providing clarification or additional explanation would greatly improve readability.
4. Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Processing
The manuscript emphasizes the importance of asynchronous processing, but the distinction from synchronous processing is not sufficiently detailed. The authors are encouraged to elaborate on the differences, including their respective advantages and disadvantages. For example, in Table 2, Peng et al. [50] report comparable performance despite not being asynchronous. Enhancing this comparison table to highlight the significance of the proposed approach would strengthen the manuscript.
5. Figure 2(A–D): Caption and Interpretation
The caption states “Analysis of model architecture and decay parameter (λ) choices on classification accuracy,” yet the figure appears to show the number of blocks versus accuracy. Does the caption misstate the content, or is there a specific relationship between λ and the number of blocks? Furthermore, the authors claim that the proposed model requires only six blocks, whereas counterparts such as ResNet require more than 30 layers. Given the distinction between the terms “block” and “layer,” is it valid to conclude that the proposed model achieves lower latency? A direct comparison in terms of latency or other performance metrics would make this claim more convincing.
6. RRAM Mapping Strategy
The authors map positive and negative weights onto separate RRAM arrays, while prior work often employs 2’s complement mapping, requiring only a single array. What motivated the use of separate arrays in this work? Discussion of the resulting area overhead and associated trade-offs would add valuable context.
7. Fixed Decay Parameter (λ) and Accuracy
Line 276 states that inference accuracy improves when fixing the decay parameter (λ). The authors should provide a more detailed mathematical derivation or theoretical explanation to clarify why and how fixing λ enhances accuracy.
8. Flexibility Limitations of Memristor Conductance Decay
Using memristor conductance decay as RN is an intriguing approach. However, because the decay rate is largely determined by oxide thickness during fabrication, flexibility may be limited for supporting different SSM models or enabling weight updates. The authors should elaborate on potential solutions to overcome this limitation, particularly given the importance of reprogramming capabilities at the edge.
9. Voltage Levels and Endurance in Conductance Updates
In Equation (9), the horizontal line voltages of the input projection memristor array are used as input spikes x(t+Δt) to update conductance. The authors should clarify the voltage levels applied in this process. Moreover, since each conductance update effectively involves multiple write operations, a discussion of endurance concerns under repeated updates would be valuable.
